lede: 23% of US wages are paid for tasks people also bring to AI models (Claude data). Pay hasn't changed more than usual, and job ads turned away from tasks AI can do from 2020 to 2022, before ChatGPT, with no further drop at its release. And 42% of new degrees are in fields that lead to the jobs most exposed to language models.

bridge.index_line: How much of the country's paid work involves tasks people already use AI for, and how many firms use it
bridge.why: If AI is going to change work, it will start with the tasks people already bring to it and the firms that adopt it, so this index shows where change could come first.

items.title: US wages paid for tasks people also bring to AI (Claude data)
items.note: Up from 18% in September 2025. A task counts once anyone uses Claude for it, so part of that rise comes from each release covering more tasks (2,051 then, 2,525 now). The tasks behind three quarters of all use, a measure that more coverage does not move, rose from 1.8% to 3.1% of US wages.
items.more: The Anthropic Economic Index sorts conversations with Claude into the job tasks the Labor Department lists for each occupation (O*NET). We add up what US workers earn on the tasks that appear, using the BLS wage tables. The June 2026 file leaves out rarely used tasks, so this figure uses March 2026, the most recent file that lists them all. Tasks people hand to Claude to do entirely account for 6% of US wages. ChatGPT is not shown here: OpenAI publishes use by broad work activity, so every task under an activity would count and the figure would not be comparable.
items.tech: Each occupation's OEWS wage bill is split across its O*NET tasks by frequency-weighted task shares, so task values sum exactly to the occupation's bill. Reach is the share of the national wage bill in tasks with any published usage, which rises mechanically with the number of tasks a release covers; the core, the smallest set of tasks covering 75% of usage (243 tasks in the latest file), does not. The published shares come without sampling errors, so no band is drawn. Claude.ai users are a selected population.

items.title: Firms using AI
items.note: 23.8% of US businesses used AI in some part of their work in the two weeks to 6 September 2026, up from 17.3% in November 2025. The band shows the Census Bureau's 95% margin of error.
items.more: The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey asks firms every two weeks whether they used AI in any of their business functions. The question took this wording in November 2025, so the series starts then; the earlier question, about AI in producing goods or services, measures something narrower and is not joined to it.
items.tech: National estimates and standard errors as published, for the share answering yes; the band is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. The survey counts firms, not workers or spending, so a small firm and a large one weigh the same.

items.title: Where AI use is heaviest
items.note: Complex problem solving skills account for 0.9% of Claude use but only 0.3% of US wages, 2.5 times as much use as their share of pay. Physical abilities get the least, 0.3 times.
items.more: We sort job tasks into 25 skill groups and compare each group's share of AI use with its share of US wages. A value above 1 means people use AI on that group's tasks more than its share of pay alone would lead you to expect. Switch between Claude and ChatGPT to compare the two platforms' users.
items.tech: Each task's labor is split across O*NET's 161 descriptors by a task-to-skill matrix built from O*NET, whose rows sum to one, and the descriptors roll up to 25 bundles, so neither usage nor wage dollars are lost in the mapping. OpenAI publishes shares by intermediate work activity, allocated here to tasks in proportion to their wage value; allocating equally instead gives the same top three groups. Claude: March 2026. ChatGPT: June 2026.

city.index_line: Whether pay, the mix of jobs and what job ads ask for have changed more than usual
city.why: If AI were already reshaping work, it would show up here first: in what employers pay for different skills, in which kinds of jobs grow, and in the tasks job ads ask for.
city.capline: Job ads: fell before ChatGPT. Pay: no unusual change. Job mix: largest shift since 2013.
city.mark: Job ads: fell before ChatGPT. Pay: no unusual change.
city.headline: Job ads turned away from tasks AI can do from 2020 to 2022, before ChatGPT, with no further drop at its release. Pay hasn't changed more than usual, and the mix of jobs has shifted more than at any time since 2013, though chance can't yet be ruled out.

items.title: Job ads for tasks AI can do
items.note: From 2020 to the third quarter of 2022, job ads in the same occupation asked less and less often for tasks AI can do. ChatGPT's release in November 2022 brought no further drop, and by the third quarter of 2025 ads had recovered 68% of the decline.
items.more: The National Labor Exchange (NLx) data count how often ads in each occupation name each O*NET task. We check whether tasks AI can do lost ground to other tasks in the same occupation, and whether anything changed at ChatGPT's release. In 25 of the 55 earlier months, the same comparison showed a change at least as large as the one at the release. Each occupation's ads list at most fifty tasks a month, so switch to complete task lists to see only the occupations where that limit never binds. What drove the fall from 2020 to 2022 is not settled here. Because the comparison is within each occupation, a shift in which occupations were hiring cannot explain it, but changes inside occupations can: the move to remote work, hiring for jobs done in person during the pandemic, and changes in which employers and job boards feed the National Labor Exchange all fall in those years.
items.tech: From a working paper in progress by the author: the gradient of a task's share of its occupation's ads on the task's Eloundou exposure, by quarter against 2019, so the comparison is within occupation by construction, with 95% bands from standard errors clustered by occupation. The step at the release is measured against the sixteen months before it and set against the same step placed at each of 55 earlier months (p = 0.45, all occupations).

items.title: Pay for different skills
items.note: If AI were changing what employers pay for, pay for some skills would be moving faster than usual. Between 2022 and 2025, none was. The biggest move, a drop in pay for analyzing information and making decisions, was smaller than the biggest move in seven of the ten earlier three-year periods since 2013. The reading for 2021 to 2024 was above the dashed line, so pay did move unusually then, but that has not carried into the latest period.
items.more: Every occupation uses a mix of 25 skill groups, from working with people to complex problem solving, as described in O*NET. From the wages BLS publishes for each occupation, we estimate what employers pay for each skill group. For each group, we compare the change over the last three years with its own changes since 2013, and call a change unusual only if it is bigger than 95% of the changes we get when we shuffle the years at random. These are averages over whole occupations, so a raise for new hires and a cut for people already in the job would cancel out.
items.tech: Relative pay is each bundle's log pay growth against the employment-weighted average, estimated for every annual transition from 2012 (13 transitions) on a balanced panel of occupations. The statistic is the largest, across the 25 bundles, of the mean of the last three transitions standardized by the bundle's own year-to-year variability. Its reference distribution relabels which three transitions are treated, using consecutive triples only, since pay changes are autocorrelated; the dashed line is that distribution's 95th percentile, and the chart divides the statistic by it, so 1.0 marks the line (p = 0.73 for the latest period).

items.title: Mix of jobs
items.note: Between 2022 and 2025, employment moved toward jobs that rely heavily on arts and humanities knowledge. It is the largest shift of all eleven three-year periods since 2013, which is as unusual as eleven periods can show. The reading for 2017 to 2020, which includes the first year of the pandemic, was also above the dashed line, so the spring 2027 wage tables will show whether this one lasts.

items.tech: The same statistic on employment-weighted bundle intensity. With 13 transitions there are 11 consecutive triples, so the smallest attainable p is 1/11; the latest period attains it (p = 0.09). The test cannot yet separate an AI effect from the post-pandemic reallocation of employment.

valley.index_line: What students choose to study, and whether young workers still get the jobs most exposed to AI
valley.exposed: Eloundou and coauthors count a task as exposed if a language model could cut the time it takes by at least half; Felten and coauthors link earlier AI applications, such as image recognition, translation and speech recognition, to the abilities a job uses. The two broadly agree (their field scores correlate at 0.7), but computer science, engineering and the social sciences count as exposed only on Eloundou's measure, and education, health and law only on Felten's. Computer science enrollment grew 42% from fall 2019 to fall 2024; leave it out and the Eloundou share falls too, from 49.6% to 49.2%.
valley.why: Students pick fields years before they work, and entry-level jobs hold many of the tasks AI can do, so the next generation of workers is where an early shift would appear.
valley.capline: 41.8% of new degrees and 53.1% of enrollment are in exposed fields; young workers down 16% in exposed jobs since 2022
valley.mark: 41.8% of new degrees are in exposed fields
valley.headline: 42% of new degrees and 53% of four-year enrollment are in the fields most exposed to language models, though on an earlier measure of AI exposure those shares are lower and falling. Young workers have lost ground in exposed jobs since 2022.

items.title: New degrees in exposed fields
items.note: 41.8% of 2025 bachelor's degrees went to the third of fields most exposed to AI on the Eloundou measure, up from 40.7% in 2024.
items.more: Degrees by field come from the Education Department's IPEDS completions files. Each field of study is scored by the AI exposure of the occupations it leads to, and the top third of fields count as exposed. The two measures disagree on direction: on Eloundou's, built for language models, the share has risen; on Felten's, built from earlier AI applications, it has fallen. Which fields count as exposed depends on the measure.
items.tech: Fields are six-digit CIP codes scored by the employment-weighted exposure of the occupations the NCES CIP-to-SOC crosswalk links them to, which records where programs are meant to lead. An ACS field-of-degree version, from where graduates actually work, is computed in the build but not yet used here. Exposed fields are the top third of fields by score, recut for each measure.

items.title: Young workers in exposed jobs
items.note: Since 2022, workers aged 22 to 27 have lost ground in the jobs most exposed to AI, by 16% compared with workers aged 35 to 54.
items.more: From the Census Bureau's monthly Current Population Survey. For each age group we divide employment in the most exposed third of jobs by employment in all other jobs, then compare the young group's ratio with the older group's. Over the last 12 months the gap was 8.4 points wider than in the months before. In 1,000 random reorderings of the months, none produced a gap that large. The data start in January 2022, so they can't show whether the decline began before ChatGPT.
items.tech: The gauge is (E_young,exposed / E_young,other) / (E_prime,exposed / E_prime,other), with composited CPS weights, exposed meaning the top third of occupations on the Eloundou measure, Census codes mapped to SOC with OEWS employment weights, and the series indexed to 2022. The permutation relabels which months count as the last twelve at the level of CPS rotation groups, so the overlap between adjacent months' samples is kept under the null. The band is plus or minus 1.96 standard errors from the random-groups method over the eight rotation groups, recomputing the gauge with each group left out.
